title: What the CMMC Pause Means for the Defense Industrial Base
gist: On July 13, 2026 the Pentagon suspended CMMC Phase II — the shift from cyber self-attestation to mandatory third-party certification — days before it would have gated CUI-handling contractors, citing paralyzing small-business costs and an assessor workforce of only 92 organizations and 633 assessors. The authors argue the real cost driver is remediating never-implemented NIST controls (SBA estimates about $594,000 total versus the Pentagon's $102,000 assessment estimate) and that CMMC in some form is inevitable, with the open questions being how and when.

insights.claim: On July 13, 2026 the Department of Defense suspended the second implementation phase of the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification program and announced a 60-day review of its future.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A dated 60-day clock whose outcome determines near-term compliance spending across thousands of defense suppliers.
insights.locator: On July 13, 2026, the Department of Defense (DOD) suspended

insights.claim: Phase II was scheduled to take effect November 10 and would have required contractors handling controlled unclassified information to obtain an assessment from an accredited certified third-party assessment organization before competing for covered contracts.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The removed gate was a hard revenue barrier — its suspension immediately relieves bid-eligibility risk for uncertified suppliers.
insights.locator: Phase II was scheduled to take effect on November 10

insights.claim: SBA Administrator Kelly Loeffler called CMMC an 'untenable barrier' while Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment Michael Duffey cited its 'paralyzing costs' and framed the suspension as part of a broader effort to cut red tape.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Two senior officials publicly against the program signals the review is likely to soften rather than restore requirements.

insights.claim: The pause suspended future milestones and required removal of C3PAO requirements from active solicitations, while contractors must still self-assess, protect CUI, submit required self-assessments, and undergo select government spot-checks.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Obligations did not disappear — only the third-party verification layer did, so cyber remediation spending remains legally required.
insights.locator: The pause delays the move from self-assessment

insights.claim: The timing reflects a broader Pentagon push to speed defense acquisition and attract commercial and nontraditional suppliers, with Duffey citing a 'strategic imperative to reduce bureaucracy.'
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Deregulation momentum favors nontraditional and venture-backed defense entrants over compliance-heavy incumbents.
insights.locator: The timing also reflects a broader Pentagon push

insights.claim: By late 2025 the CMMC ecosystem had only 92 approved assessment organizations and 633 certified assessors, and the GAO warned the Pentagon had not shown this workforce could meet demand.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Quantifies the supply bottleneck: an assessor market this thin is both the reason for the pause and a growth market if CMMC returns.
insights.quote: By late 2025, however, the system had only 92 approved assessment organizations and 633 certified assessors.
insights.locator: The phased schedule was intended to give contractors time

insights.claim: Phase II implementation might have necessitated issuing a large number of waivers to avoid disrupting ongoing Pentagon procurement, but the GAO warned that relying on waivers to manage assessor shortages would undermine the program's core purpose.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The choice was mass waivers or a pause — both mean the certification regime cannot be enforced at current capacity.
insights.locator: The pause followed months of discussions

insights.claim: The Pentagon estimated an initial Level 2 third-party assessment and affirmation would cost a small company approximately $102,000, including roughly $31,000 paid to the assessment organization plus the contractor's preparation, documentation, and participation time.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The $31,000 assessor fee is the actual addressable revenue per small-supplier certification for C3PAO firms.
insights.quote: The Pentagon estimated that an initial Level 2 third-party assessment and affirmation would cost a small company approximately $102,000, including roughly $31,000 paid to the assessment organization
insights.locator: The Pentagon estimated that an initial Level 2

insights.claim: The Pentagon's $102,000 estimate excludes the cost of buying new systems, hiring security staff, and bringing a deficient network into compliance because it assumes the underlying NIST controls are already implemented, and the SBA estimates total costs can reach about $594,000.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The nearly 6x gap between DOD and SBA cost estimates is the crux of the political fight and the size of the latent cyber-remediation market.
insights.quote: The SBA estimates that total costs can reach about $594,000.
insights.locator: Such remediation can be more expensive than the assessment

insights.claim: Critics of CMMC conflate the cost of an outside assessment with the far larger cost of actually meeting cybersecurity standards that contractors handling CUI have been legally required to implement since 2017.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Reframes the debate: pausing certification does not erase a nine-year-old legal obligation, so liability exposure persists for non-compliant firms.
insights.quote: although some conflate the cost of an outside assessment with the more significant cost of actually meeting the cybersecurity standards
insights.locator: Critics have argued that CMMC risks shutting small suppliers out

insights.claim: Remediation to reach compliance may require investment in new databases, login tools, network segmentation, encryption, or a separate CUI environment, followed by recurring expenses for licenses, cloud hosting, monitoring, patching, managed services, training, and cybersecurity personnel.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Enumerates the recurring-revenue product categories that benefit whenever CMMC enforcement resumes — MSSPs, GovCloud, identity tooling.
insights.locator: A contractor may need to invest in new databases

insights.claim: During rulemaking industry commenters asked the Pentagon to declare reassessment and recertification expenses reimbursable and the Pentagon declined, meaning fixed-price contractors must build expected CMMC expenses into future bids while cost-reimbursement contractors may charge allowable cybersecurity costs to the government.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Contract-type mix becomes a margin variable: fixed-price-heavy suppliers absorb compliance costs directly against margin.
insights.locator: Another controversy concerns reimbursement.

insights.claim: Non-reimbursability creates a competition problem because a company seeking its first defense award must finance new systems, training, and an assessment before it can compete, giving incumbents with already compliant networks an asymmetric advantage.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: CMMC functions as an entry moat for compliant incumbents — its suspension is competitively negative for them and positive for new entrants.
insights.locator: Non-reimbursability may also create competition problems.

insights.claim: Prime contractors and government solicitations have increasingly imposed CMMC Level 2 requirements on small business subcontractors even where their work does not currently involve CUI access, because uncertainty about future CUI sharing pushes primes toward a very broad compliance scope as risk mitigation.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Flow-down over-scoping means the true compliance market is far larger than DOD's own Level 1/Level 2 population estimates.
insights.locator: While CMMC Level 1 requirements were intended to be sufficient

insights.claim: Some DOD program offices have started putting CMMC Level 2 assessment requirements into solicitations this year, ahead of the formal phase schedule.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: De facto enforcement was running ahead of the official timeline, so the pause has real near-term bid-eligibility effects.

insights.claim: For eight years the government largely relied on contractors self-reporting NIST compliance with thin oversight, and a 2022 DOD inspector general review of 10 research contractors found all 10 in violation of NIST standards.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A 10-of-10 failure rate is the empirical basis for third-party verification and the reason CMMC will return in some form.
insights.quote: A 2022 DOD inspector general review of 10 research contractors found all in violation of NIST standards.
insights.locator: For eight years, the government largely relied on contractors

insights.claim: Because even small suppliers may hold critical data or connect to larger defense networks, a weakness at one company can create risk throughout the supply chain, and small business status does not reduce the national security damage of stolen weapons data, production information, or software.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The security logic is unaffected by the cost debate, which is why relief is likely to come as subsidy rather than exemption.
insights.locator: Because even small suppliers may hold critical data

insights.claim: CMMC 2.0, finalized in 2024, reduced the number of certification levels, expanded self-assessments, and reserved outside reviews for contractors handling more sensitive information after the 2019 first version drew criticism for cost and complexity.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The program has already been softened once under cost pressure — a precedent for how the 60-day review will likely resolve.
insights.locator: The first version of CMMC, announced in 2019

insights.claim: CMMC's three levels map to escalating requirements: Level 1 covers Federal Contract Information under FAR clause 52.204-21, Level 2 applies to firms processing, storing or transmitting CUI under NIST SP 800-171.3, and Level 3 covers high-priority programs facing advanced persistent threats under NIST SP 800-172.3 with a government-led assessment.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The level map determines which suppliers face six-figure remediation versus basic hygiene — the key segmentation for compliance vendors.
insights.locator: CMMC has three levels of cybersecurity requirements

insights.claim: Defense contractors face state-sponsored efforts to obtain sensitive military and technological information through phishing and exploitation of software misconfigurations, which is why NIST SP 800-171.3 protections covering personnel training, two-factor authentication and risk monitoring have grown in importance.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The underlying threat is escalating regardless of regulatory posture, so cyber spend in the defense base is secularly rising.
insights.locator: Such protections have become increasingly important

themes.theme: What comes next: reform task force and subsidy paths

insights.claim: The DOD chief information officer established a CMMC Reform Task Force and issued an industry request for information; the task force met first on July 16 and plans a public report at the end of the 60-day review.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A dated public report is the next catalyst that will reprice compliance-services demand across the defense supply base.
insights.locator: The DOD’s chief information officer has established

insights.claim: The clearest path to address small business concerns is loan or grant programs for upfront certification costs, such as an SBA program offering 10-year loans repaid through contract rates or forgiven against performance targets.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Subsidized financing would convert the cost objection into a funded demand stream for cybersecurity vendors rather than killing it.
insights.locator: The clearest path to address small business concerns

insights.claim: Connecticut's Cybersecurity Adoption Program, Massachusetts's Manufacturing Cybersecurity Program, and Oregon's Advanced Manufacturing Federal Contract Competitiveness Funding all already list CMMC compliance as grant-eligible, providing state-level templates for federal replication.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Three named state programs are existing funding channels for cyber-readiness vendors selling into small defense manufacturers.
insights.locator: Several states have created grants or cost-sharing programs

insights.claim: Excessive designation of data as CUI pulls unnecessary systems and employees into the assessment boundary, so DOD could refine covered-system definitions, discourage primes from over-flowing Level 2 requirements, and clarify reimbursement eligibility.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Scope narrowing, not repeal, is the most likely reform lever — it shrinks per-firm cost without weakening the standard.
insights.locator: Excessive designation of data as CUI

insights.claim: The underlying need for defense sector cybersecurity is widely acknowledged and growing, so CMMC in one form or another will happen and the only open questions are how and when.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Treat the pause as a delay, not a cancellation — compliance-services demand is deferred rather than destroyed.
insights.quote: To meet this strategic necessity, CMMC—in one form or another—will happen. The open questions are how and when.
insights.locator: While CMMC’s rollout has been heavily criticized
